description: We are a group of software engineers who like to solve real-life problems.
summary:
SELENE OPS is a web app that answers the question every lunar south pole mission must solve: where and when can a lander land and survive? Near the pole the Sun stays a few degrees above the horizon, so mountains and crater rims decide whether solar panels get light and whether Earth is in view for communication.

Pick one of NASA's nine Artemis candidate regions (or any point between 80° and 90°S), choose a CLPS or HLS lander, and set a landing window. SELENE OPS simulates sunlight, Earth visibility, battery charge and night heating hour by hour, using NASA LRO LOLA terrain and JPL ephemerides, and returns a clear verdict — feasible or not, the probability of success, and the best landing date across 2026–2035. A replay shows the mission: shadows move, the battery drains and recharges.

We validated the model against JPL Horizons and NASA's LOLA illumination maps, reproduced the real IM-2 Athena landing, and show the trade-off between sunlight for survival and proximity to permanently shadowed craters that may hold water ice.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SELENE OPS is a landing-window planner for the lunar south pole. A mission planner chooses a site (one of NASA's nine Artemis III candidate regions, or any point between 80° and 90°S), a lander (CLPS: Nova-C, Blue Ghost, Griffin; HLS: Starship HLS, Blue Moon Mk2) and a landing window. The app simulates the mission hour by hour and returns a verdict in plain language: feasible, marginal or not feasible, why, the probability of success, and the best landing date between 2026 and 2035.

Try it: https://selene.byst.re/ — press "Quick demo" for a guided example: a lander rides out a period of darkness on its battery, and the same site a few weeks later, where the mission is lost. On a first visit the 3D terrain takes a few seconds to load.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Terrain and horizons: from the NASA LRO LOLA polar elevation model we compute, for every site, the true horizon in 360 directions (out to 150 km, with lunar curvature).

2. Sun and Earth: JPL DE421 ephemerides and NAIF lunar orientation kernels (via Skyfield) give the Sun and Earth direction for every hour from 2026 to 2035. Comparing them with the horizon gives the visible fraction of the solar disk and whether Earth is in view.

3. Landing sites: real candidate landing spots inside the Artemis regions from Wueller et al. (2026, JGR Planets); for each region we select the best-lit spot that passes a slope filter.

4. Mission simulation (in the browser): fixed solar panels with the real Sun incidence angle, battery with round-trip efficiency, day and survival loads, night heaters driven by LRO Diviner ground temperatures. Every lander figure has a source link or is clearly marked as an assumption.

5. Optimizer: every landing day in the window is simulated for all nine regions and shown as a heatmap.

6. Uncertainty: a Monte Carlo over landing point (each lander's landing accuracy), loads and heading gives P(FEASIBLE) instead of a single yes/no.

7. Custom points: any point in 80–90°S is analysed directly in the browser from a downsampled LOLA terrain model and hourly ephemerides.

VALIDATION

- Sun and Earth directions match JPL Horizons to within 0.005°.

- Compared like for like with NASA's LOLA illumination maps (Mazarico et al. 2011) at their own pixel centres, our sunlit fraction differs on average by 0.1–4.1 percentage points per site.

- All nine regions meet NASA's statement that each contains locations with continuous sunlight for 6.5 days.

- The in-browser method for custom points agrees with the pipeline within about 2 percentage points.

- Case study IM-2 Athena (March 2025): we re-ran the planned and the actual landing spot. Both had full sunlight and Earth in view; our model shows the outcome depended on the lander's orientation (it landed on its side), and that its battery alone could last 9–14 hours — Athena operated for about 12.75 hours.

- Over 100 unit tests and browser tests in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit run before every deployment.

SCIENCE: SUNLIGHT VS WATER ICE

The south pole matters because permanently shadowed craters may hold water ice — but those same shadows threaten survival. Using NASA's LOLA map of permanently shadowed regions, the app shows the distance to the nearest cold trap and the trade-off between a sunnier site and one closer to ice, with a full verdict for the "ice-first" spot in each region.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Turns complex illumination data into a decision a mission team, student or the public can understand in seconds.

- Shows that the landing date matters as much as the site: the same place can be safe one week and fatal three weeks later.

- Transparent: each number shows whether it is sourced, derived or assumed.

- Open source and reproducible: the same inputs always give the same output.

CREATIVITY

A cinematic 3D view of the real south-pole terrain where the lander touches down, followed by a time-lapse replay of the mission driven by the actual ephemerides — moving shadows, a battery gauge and Earth contact — so the analysis can be seen, not only read. A surface view shows the Earth, Sun and stars exactly where the data puts them — Earth sinking behind the mountains explains a loss of contact at a glance.

TOOLS

C# / .NET Blazor WebAssembly, CesiumJS (Cesium Moon terrain), Python (Skyfield, NumPy, rasterio), xUnit, pytest, Playwright, GitHub Actions, nginx. AI tools: Claude Code (code, tests, documentation), Meshy AI and Microsoft TRELLIS.2 (stylised 3D lander models, marked "AI-generated" in the app). All scientific values come from NASA/JPL data computed by our code, not from AI.

LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

Lander power and load figures are partly estimates where manufacturers publish none (clearly marked). The model computes lighting, power and heat; it cannot predict landing failures such as tipping over. Next: higher-resolution terrain near the pole, communication through specific ground stations, rover traverse planning.

The name comes from Selene, the Greek goddess of the Moon. Not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.
